steps.title: Sharpen the brief
steps.prompt: Use sharpen on this brief: build a local reading-list app where I can add a URL, mark it read, and find it again. Keep the scope small. Leave framework and storage choices open. Return the four framing answers and a rewritten prompt, then stop.
steps.output: A clearer brief. Sharpen does not create files or execute the project.

steps.title: Build one complete journey
steps.prompt: Use poteto-mode to implement the reading-list brief above in this empty project folder. Inspect available tools and agree any unresolved product choices first. Build add, list, mark-read, and search with browser-local storage. Keep this local. Use existing dependencies where possible; ask before installations or external actions.

steps.title: Check the delivered app
steps.prompt: Use principle-prove-it-works on the reading-list app. Add an item through the UI, mark it read, reload, and search for it. Check an empty list and invalid input. Report observed results and anything you could not run.

workflows.principle: Prove it works: finishing the code is followed by exercising what the user receives.

workflows.title: Add a small feature to an existing app
workflows.goal: Add a status filter to a task list without changing how tasks are stored.

steps.title: Find the current behavior
steps.prompt: Use how to trace this task list from its route through data loading to rendering. Identify status values, existing filter behavior, and relevant checks. Keep this read-only and cite the source files.
steps.output: A short map of the code that owns the feature.

steps.title: Implement the bounded change
steps.prompt: Add an All / Open / Done filter to the existing task list. Follow its current UI conventions and preserve storage and API contracts. Handle empty filtered results. Use blast-radius to inspect affected callers and run the existing focused checks.
steps.output: A focused change with caller impact and empty-state behavior checked.

workflows.principle: Subtract before you add: reuse the existing task status and filtering logic before introducing another representation.
workflows.done: Each filter displays the right tasks, and clearing it restores the original list.

workflows.title: Fix a reproducible bug
workflows.goal: A whitespace-only search hides every result instead of showing the full list.

steps.title: Reproduce and fix
steps.prompt: Use tdd to fix this bug: a search containing only spaces hides all items; it should behave like an empty search. Find the existing cheap local test target, demonstrate the failure before the fix, trace the input-handling cause, then make the smallest correction and rerun the check. If the test path is unavailable, state that limit instead of inventing a result.
steps.output: A failing-before and passing-after regression check, or an explicit account of the missing evidence.

steps.title: Check neighboring behavior
steps.prompt: Use principle-fix-root-causes to review the search fix. Check empty input, leading and trailing spaces, a real query, and no matches. Confirm that normalization happens at the correct boundary and report the checks actually run.
steps.output: A verified correction with nearby behavior covered.

workflows.principle: Fix root causes: correct input handling where the bad state first enters the search flow.
workflows.done: The original reproduction passes and normal search still works.

workflows.title: Start a project with a deliberate architecture
workflows.goal: Create a small team issue tracker with clear ownership and a repeatable verification workflow.

steps.title: Define a useful first release
steps.prompt: Use sharpen on this project brief: a team issue tracker with project lists, issue creation, and status changes. Ask for evidence that the core journey works. Keep authentication provider, framework, hosting, and paid services as open choices. Rewrite the brief and stop.
steps.output: A bounded first-release brief and explicit unresolved product choices.

steps.title: Sketch the design before implementation
steps.prompt: Use architect on the issue-tracker brief. Compare two ownership models for projects, issues, and memberships. Sketch caller usage, types, module boundaries, and allowed issue transitions. Read the available host contracts. Keep this design-only; do not install dependencies or implement yet.
steps.output: A concrete design with tradeoffs and an implementation boundary.

steps.title: Implement the selected slice
steps.prompt: Use poteto-mode to implement the selected issue-tracker design. Start with create-project, create-issue, and change-status as one complete slice. Keep ownership and validation at explicit boundaries. Inspect existing tooling and obtain authorization before adding dependencies or services. Report deviations from the design.
steps.output: A working first slice with scoped changes and observed checks.

steps.title: Leave reusable checks
steps.prompt: Use create-verification-skill for the issue tracker. Inspect the app's real commands and available browser/test tools. Define observable checks for issue creation, status changes, invalid input, and project separation. Run the supported checks and identify unavailable ones. Verify local skill discovery separately from writing the file.

workflows.principle: Model the domain: represent issue states and membership rules explicitly before wiring screens together.
workflows.done: The first slice is usable, its boundaries are reviewable, and another agent can rerun the documented checks.

workflows.title: Add a feature across UI and API boundaries
workflows.goal: Add project-scoped CSV export without exposing another project's records.

steps.title: Trace access before adding output
steps.prompt: Use how to trace project membership checks, list queries, and file responses in this app. Find the existing authorization boundary and cite its callers. Keep this read-only.
steps.output: A map of the access rules the export must preserve.

steps.title: Design and implement within scope
steps.prompt: Use architect to compare synchronous and queued CSV export for the actual data sizes and existing infrastructure. State the tradeoffs, then implement the simplest supported design for project-scoped issue export. Reuse current membership checks, validate inputs, and handle an empty export. Do not add services or paid dependencies without approval.
steps.output: An export implementation whose design matches observed needs.

steps.title: Review the boundary
steps.prompt: Use blast-radius to trace the export change's callers and authorization assumptions. Use interrogate for an adversarial review of cross-project access and malformed inputs. Exercise the real API with allowed and denied project access. If independent reviewers are unavailable, disclose reduced capability and keep review claims bounded.
steps.output: Evidence for allowed exports and denied access, plus unresolved risks.

workflows.principle: Boundary discipline: enforce project access where data leaves the application, using the existing authorization contract.
workflows.done: An authorized user can export their project's records; a user without access cannot.

workflows.title: Diagnose a bug that spans several components
workflows.goal: An issue looks updated in the UI but returns to its old status after a refresh.

steps.title: Trace the failed journey
steps.prompt: Use how to trace a status change through the UI, request, validation, database update, and cache refresh. Reproduce the stale-status bug through actual entry points where authorized. Separate observed behavior from hypotheses and retain relevant evidence without secrets.
steps.output: A reproduction and a ranked account of where the state diverges.

steps.title: Fix the owning component
steps.prompt: Use poteto-mode to fix the reproduced stale-status bug at its root cause. Use show-me-your-work to retain a local decision trail. Avoid compensating UI changes if persistence is wrong. Add a focused regression check when practical, run blast-radius on the affected callers, and verify the status after a reload.
steps.output: A scoped fix, an inspected user journey, and a reviewable local log.

workflows.principle: Attack the premise: if repeated fixes fail the same check, revisit the shared assumption before adding another patch.
workflows.done: The updated status survives a reload, and the evidence identifies the component that caused the failure.

workflows.title: Coordinate a migration with independent work
workflows.goal: Move a legacy notification system behind one new interface while preserving existing callers.

steps.title: Set ownership and migration order
steps.prompt: Use architect to map notification callers and design the replacement interface from caller usage. Plan a migration that moves callers before deleting the old API. Identify independent slices, file ownership, integration order, and user-visible checks. Keep implementation paused until the design is reviewed.
steps.output: A caller map, selected design, and conflict-aware work plan.

steps.title: Execute isolated slices
steps.prompt: Use swarm to implement the reviewed notification migration. Assign disjoint caller groups to isolated workers with explicit boundaries; keep one integration owner. Use show-me-your-work for decisions and inspect every worker's terminal result and artifact before integration. If workers or isolation are unavailable, disclose the limit and use a sequential plan without claiming independent execution.
steps.output: Integrated changes with actual worker receipts, or an explicitly sequential result.

steps.title: Remove the old path and verify
steps.prompt: Use blast-radius to find remaining legacy notification callers. Remove the obsolete API only after callers have migrated. Run the checks that observe delivery, failure handling, and retries using isolated test data. Report any integration that could not be exercised.
steps.output: A coherent migration with the old path removed and remaining gaps stated.

workflows.principle: Separate before serializing shared state: give workers isolated outputs and one explicit integration point.
workflows.done: Callers use the selected interface, obsolete code is removed, and supported journeys pass the recorded checks.

workflows.title: Investigate a retry or concurrency failure
workflows.goal: Two retrying workers can process the same job and produce a duplicate result.

steps.title: Check one important property
steps.prompt: Use create-formal-verification-skill to investigate duplicate job completion under retries. Start from the real claim, lock, and completion code. Choose a suitable verifier, state the property and bounds, and cite the code each model action represents. Use an already authorized local toolchain; do not install tools implicitly. Run deliberate broken-code trials only in an owned disposable copy. If no verifier can run, label any generated-input testing as a testing fallback, not formal proof.
steps.output: A bounded verification result or an explicit block, with a runnable local skill when supported.

steps.title: Explain the failure as a user story
steps.prompt: Use statechart on the job-processing model. Show states in terms of what the operator sees, retain invariants and code-guard citations, and turn each counterexample into a numbered story. Use an authorized local renderer and inspect every SVG. Replay the story through the real application's entry points; distinguish modeled behavior from reproduced behavior. Do not fix product code in this step.
steps.output: Mermaid charts, compiler reports and separately rendered SVGs with model scope and reproduction status separated.

steps.title: Recheck after an authorized fix
steps.prompt: After the job-processing fix is separately implemented and authorized, use maintain-formal-verification-skill to reconcile the verification with the changed code. Preserve the original property, inspect covered functions, rerun checks, demonstrate the check still detects a relevant broken variant in isolation, and advance the sync record only for code actually checked.
steps.output: Verification that describes the current implementation, with explicit bounds and remaining findings.

workflows.principle: Explain the number: a model pass covers its stated bounds and assumptions; it is not a claim that the whole production system is correct.
workflows.done: The model and real-code evidence are separately reviewable. Missing tools, citations, rendering, or reproduction leave the dependent result incomplete.

workflows.title: Review a release before asking to publish
workflows.goal: Assess an existing feature branch against its acceptance criteria and user journeys.

steps.title: Challenge the completed change
steps.prompt: Use interrogate and blast-radius to review this feature branch against the supplied acceptance criteria. Trace affected callers, challenge data and authorization assumptions, and distinguish confirmed defects from untested risks. Report actual reviewer independence and model identity only when observed.
steps.output: A prioritized review tied to code and acceptance criteria.

steps.title: Verify and prepare the handoff
steps.prompt: Use maintain-verification-skill to check whether this project's verification workflow still matches its actual UI, API, and commands. Run the supported release checks. Use technical-writing to prepare release notes with changes, observed results, and unresolved gaps. Keep deployment and publication paused for explicit authorization.
steps.output: A release handoff that states what is checked and what remains open.

workflows.principle: Outcome-oriented execution: the release decision follows the requested behavior and evidence, rather than a completed checklist alone.
workflows.done: The user can review the release evidence and make a concrete publication decision.

# pstack-openai

An unofficial port of Lauren Tan's pstack. Candidate 0.2.4 adapts the combined compiler, review and orchestration changes from upstream v0.15.36. Its inventory records 573 source files and 58 canonical roots, including one deferred reference. The runtime package retains 57 skills, 24 principles and 23 playbooks. Read [UPSTREAM.md](UPSTREAM.md), [NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md) and [LICENSE](LICENSE) for lineage and attribution.

Accepted baseline 0.2.3 remains upstream `4ec7ffa173eaa70d3d9467a627baf0954645a353` as the reviewed source baseline. Candidate source `c742dd61706fbacc1b95f1a20b7b988cf096ce6c` is staged and unaccepted. See [source acceptance and verification limits](docs/releases/0.2.3.md). Installed discovery and workflow support remain separate gates.

Upstream adds Claude Code packaging; this port retains its shared portable runtime and records the Claude adapter as a quoted reference only.

It also makes `/sharpen` return four framing answers and a rewritten prompt without executing its task. It adds create-formal-verification-skill and maintain-formal-verification-skill, including bounded claims, safe mutation trials and explicit testing fallbacks. Source validation and installed discovery are tracked separately from full workflow behavior. The [0.2.2 source validation record](docs/releases/0.2.2.md) identifies the reviewed snapshot, checks and remaining host limits. Earlier release records retain their historical scope. See [compatibility](docs/compatibility.md) before relying on a workflow.

## What it does

- Routes engineering tasks through a playbook with `poteto-mode`.
- Compares alternative implementations with `arena`, or divides independent work with `swarm` when the host supports workers.
- Explains code and design decisions with `how`, `why`, and `teach`.
- Reviews changes with `interrogate` and checks affected code with `blast-radius`.
- Adds verification workflows and removes formulaic wording with `unslop`.

Candidate navigation is frozen with operative content. The final handoff must keep these bytes unchanged or explicitly refreeze and relink fresh blocked observations. Evidence/report commits can follow the tested commit only under the exact [tested-package marker contract](docs/maintenance/rollback.md). After blocked host records enter the inventory and regenerate the catalog, an explicit second freeze is required. Fresh blocked discovery records must then name that final SHA. No behavioral pass transfers between freezes.

Use [`/statechart`](skills/statechart/SKILL.md) to check a TLA+ model and draw flat, parent or region charts using a reviewed view. The compiler retires automatic chart-to-spec conversion and integrated comparison flags. [Execution prerequisites](skills/statechart/references/execution.md) are explicit; unavailable tools leave verification blocked.

## Workflow examples

Choose a scenario and send its prompts in order. Review each result before continuing. These examples describe intended outputs, not observed host results. Check [compatibility](docs/compatibility.md) for available tools and current verification limits.

Keep one controller responsible for the task. Workers, isolation, tool installation, external actions, and publication require the relevant host capabilities and authorization.

- [Simple](#simple-workflows): start a small project from scratch; add a small feature to an existing app; fix a reproducible bug.
- [Intermediate](#intermediate-workflows): start a project with a deliberate architecture; add a feature across UI and API boundaries; diagnose a bug that spans several components.
- [Advanced](#advanced-workflows): coordinate a migration with independent work; investigate a retry or concurrency failure; review a release before asking to publish.

Use interrogate and blast-radius to review this feature branch against the supplied acceptance criteria. Trace affected callers, challenge data and authorization assumptions, and distinguish confirmed defects from untested risks. Report actual reviewer independence and model identity only when observed.
```

```

---
name: architect
description: "Sketch types, signatures, and module structure before code, then stay in the loop while implementation fills in. Use for /architect, 'architect this', 'design this', or non-trivial work where jumping to code would lock in the wrong shape."

# Architect

Design before implementing. Sketch types, function signatures, class shapes, and module boundaries with `not implemented` bodies and pseudocode. Synthesize across multiple model perspectives, then fill in code against the chosen sketch. If implementation proves the sketch wrong, throw it out and redesign.

## Start

Open a todolist with one entry per phase before starting. If no task-list tool is exposed, keep the same phase list in the response and disclose that limit.

1. Ground
2. Sketch
3. Agree
4. Implement
5. Scrap

## Session capabilities and authorization

Read [host capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md), [model roles](../../references/model-roles.md) and the [assignment contract](../../references/orchestration-contract.md). Use only observed exposed tools within user authorization. Read and follow each required skill in full. If direct invocation is unavailable, disclose that limit and execute its complete workflow inline as reduced capability. A missing required skill remains blocked. Record worker identities, requested and observed selections, rejections, result artifacts and limits.

Independent exploration requires authorized workers with observed spawn and result inspection. Without workers, disclose reduced capability and produce at least two sequential, structurally distinct alternatives using the complete arena workflow and runner discipline. Sequential alternatives are not independent model perspectives. Unverified or identical observed models do not establish model diversity. Denied source reads block grounding; denied writes leave a read-only design and an explicit implementation block.

## Phase A: Ground the problem

Build a real mental model of every system the new code touches. Run the **how** skill over the relevant subsystems.

Naming a file isn't grounding. Produce the traced model `how` prescribes. If the design redefines ownership or layering, also run the **why** skill on the existing shape so the rationale becomes a constraint, not a guess.

Skip Phase A only when the work is genuinely greenfield with no surrounding system to integrate.

## Phase B: Sketch

Run the **arena** skill with the design-sketch task and the Phase A grounding artifacts. Pass `references/runner-prompt.md` as each runner's prompt. Each candidate produces a design package shaped per `references/rationale-template.md`.

Take runner preferences from an available user-supplied `architect runners` configuration, in place of arena runner preferences. When no architect runner preferences are supplied, request inherited selection per the model-role contract. Preserve the goal of distinct model perspectives when supported and verified; inheritance does not establish diversity. Resolve aliases and rejected entries through the complete **arena** Phase A rules and current model-role contract. Select explicit models only when the exposed operation supports them; otherwise disclose inherited selection and unverified diversity. If an exact selection is required but unavailable, block that selection instead of silently replacing it.

Design it twice. Require at least two structurally distinct candidates before synthesis, even when the first looks sufficient. This is the **exhaust-the-design-space** principle skill made concrete. Whole-shape alternatives, not point fixes inside one shape.

Screen every candidate against [`references/design-red-flags.md`](references/design-red-flags.md) before synthesis. Assume the next contributor is an agent that sees only the files it opened, copies the nearest example, and takes the shortest path that compiles. Prefer the design where a change that looks right from one file is right for the whole repo.

Compare viable candidates on interface depth. Prefer the design that hides more complexity behind a smaller, simpler public surface. A rich interface can keep call chains short by concentrating capability instead of scattering it across layers.

Arena returns one synthesized design package. The synthesis decision populates the rationale's "Synthesis decision" section.

## Phase C: Agree (opt-in)

Default: proceed directly to implementation with the synthesized design when implementation is already authorized. No additional human checkpoint. Design-only scope does not authorize implementation.

Opt in to a checkpoint when the invoker explicitly asks: "/architect with checkpoint," "stop and show me before implementing," or similar. Then surface the synthesized design and pause for sign-off.

With explicit commit authorization, the synthesis can ship as its own commit either way, as the "scaffold first" mode of the **foundational-thinking** principle skill. Planned and scoped breakage during fill-in is fine, per the **outcome-oriented-execution** principle skill. For adversarial pressure on the design before implementing, run the **interrogate** skill on the synthesized sketch.

If the human pushes back on the shape (in a checkpoint or after the fact), treat that as Phase A evidence. Re-ground and re-run Phase B before writing more code.

## Phase D: Implement against the sketch

Replace `not implemented` bodies with code, pseudocode with logic. The synthesized sketch is the contract.

Deviations from the sketch are signal worth surfacing, not friction to absorb silently. If a function needs a parameter the sketch didn't anticipate, ask whether the sketch was wrong, the requirement was missed, or the implementation is overreaching.

## Phase E: Scrap when the architecture is wrong

If implementation keeps producing friction the sketch can't absorb, throw the sketch out. Don't bolt fixes onto a wrong design, per the **redesign-from-first-principles** and **fix-root-causes** principle skills.

The signal is a *pattern*, not single instances. Tells:

- The same shape of workaround appearing repeatedly across unrelated code.
- Multiple unrelated edge cases that all need special-case branches.
- Types that need escape hatches (`any`, casts, optional fields always set in practice) to compile.
- The "we need a lock" reflex when the sketch said the state wasn't shared.
- Callers having to know the abstraction's internal rules to use it.
- Two or more independent Phase D deviations of the same shape across the implementation.

Use judgment. A few edge cases don't condemn an architecture. Some problems are legitimately complex. Complexity in the data is not complexity in the design.

When you scrap:

1. Re-run the **how** skill over what's been built.
2. Redesign as if the new constraints had been day-one assumptions, per redesign-from-first-principles.
3. Subtract before adding, per the **subtract-before-you-add** principle skill. The new sketch should be smaller than the old one before it grows.
4. Return to Phase B and re-run arena.

## Outputs

The caller's usage is written first and the type sketch derived from it. One file with new types and signatures for small changes. Module map plus type definitions for larger work. The rationale ships alongside, shaped per `references/rationale-template.md`, including the usage sketch and the synthesis decision.

Apply [unslop](../unslop/SKILL.md) to generated rationale and reports without changing facts or principle meanings.

---
name: arena
description: "Spawn N parallel candidates at the same task, pick a base, graft the strongest parts of the losers into it. Use for /arena, 'arena this', 'throw it in the arena', or when one attempt at a non-trivial artifact would lock in the wrong shape."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Arena

Read [session capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md), [model roles](../../references/model-roles.md), [assignment and integration](../../references/orchestration-contract.md), and [workflow ownership](../../references/workflow-ownership.md). Use only exposed, authorized operations. Read each applied principle leaf in full before dependent work. Missing required reads block that work. Invocation aliases are guidance, not proof of registered host commands.

Independent candidates and a fresh independent judge require observed worker operations and inspected artifacts. If unavailable, produce authorized sequential alternatives and parent comparison only as reduced capability. Do not claim independence, background execution, model diversity or a full arena pass. If independence is required, leave that gate blocked.

Fan out N parallel attempts at the same task. Read every candidate end to end. Pick the strongest as the base. Graft the best ideas from the others into it. Verify the synthesized result.

## Start

Open an exposed todo list with one entry per phase before launching anything. Without one, use an authorized local Markdown checklist and disclose the reduced binding.

1. Frame
2. Fan out
3. Cross-judge
4. Pick
5. Graft
6. Verify

## Phase A: Frame

The N candidates will receive the same prompt, so the prompt is the contract.

1. State the artifact each candidate is producing.
2. Derive the rubric. State what success looks like for *this* task, then turn it into 3-6 concrete gradeable criteria. The rubric is the picker's tool in Phase D. Candidates only see the task.
3. Pick the runners. Use an explicitly supplied, authorized `arena runners` preference if available. Otherwise request two inherited workers, one per seat. The source defaults used two specific model families. Their source-host slugs are not portable availability evidence. Select an explicit model or effort only from current exposed documentation or observed enumeration under the model-role contract. An `auto` or `inherit-parent` entry means omit explicit model selection. On rejection, record it and disclose a supported same-family alternative when available, otherwise an authorized inherited alternative. If the exact model is required, block instead. Record requested and observed model and effort separately, using unknown when unobserved. More seats can cover multiple design directions. Same model N times is appropriate when work is generation-bound rather than judgment-sensitive. Unknown models leave diversity unverified.
4. Assign output paths. Each candidate writes to its own authorized location, a git worktree where supported, otherwise a distinct local candidate directory. Follow [separate-before-serializing-shared-state](../principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state/SKILL.md). Confirm isolation and write permissions before dispatch. Record immutable assignment identity, input SHA, owner, role and evidence links under the assignment contract. Workers never integrate shared files. Worktree creation and persistence require observed authorized capabilities.

## Phase B: Fan out

Dispatch all N independent candidates together through the exposed worker operation, using observed background execution when available. Give each the same task, shared grounding path, its isolated output path, and instructions to produce both the artifact and a short rationale. Withhold the rubric from candidates. Inspect terminal results and artifact paths before accepting completion; a wait notification alone is insufficient.

A fresh worker can still inherit the parent's conversation, including its rubric. Use an exposed context-isolation setting for blind candidates, such as `fork_turns: "none"` where the host documents it, and inspect that dispatch setting. Asking a worker to ignore inherited grading cues does not remove exposure. If isolation is unavailable, disclose that limit and withhold the blind comparison claim. Quarantine exposed attempts rather than relabeling them as blind; any replacement gets a new immutable assignment and its own output path.

Each rationale names the alternatives the candidate considered and what it rejected.

If a configured runner is rejected, record the rejected selection and never retry it unchanged. Use only a documented supported and authorized same-family fallback, or drop the seat when none is available. Replace dropped seats up to the configured count, or the two-seat default, using an authorized surviving selection or inheritance. Disclose replacement models and preserve explicit exact-model requirements as blocked. Each replacement gets a fresh immutable assignment and output owner. Never replace a writer until its terminal state or safe quarantine is inspected. If execution leaves fewer than two completed candidates, label incomplete competition. Zero survivors blocks synthesis. Never integrate partial or cancelled artifacts as completed candidates.

## Phase C: Cross-judge

After all Phase B candidates reach terminal state and their accepted artifacts are inspected, inspect the authorized cross-judge pool in preference order. A judge must use an observed model family different from the parent's. An auto or inherit-parent alias never judges. Do not infer a family from a source-host alias or invent model mappings. Try only currently supported, authorized selections and track rejected entries so no rejected model is retried. Preserve exact-model requirements.

Spawn one fresh readonly judge only when a different family is supported. Give it the rubric and completed artifacts by path label. Verify actual parent and judge model families in the result before accepting the independent cross-family claim. If the selected model resolves to the parent's family, quarantine that verdict. Unknown observed families leave that gate unverified. If no different-family judge can run, skip judging, let the parent choose alone, and label the result reduced capability. Do not replace it with an inherited or same-family judge. A required independent or cross-family gate remains blocked.

The judge scores each criterion and recommends a base with rationale. It has no candidate write ownership and never starts while candidates are still writing. Its missing or unverified verdict must remain explicit in the synthesis record.

## Phase D: Pick a base

Read every candidate end to end before picking.

Score each candidate against the rubric criterion by criterion, not on holistic feel. Compare against the cross-judge when a verified judge ran. Otherwise record parent-only selection and reduced capability. Agreement on the base confirms the pick. Disagreement means one of you is biased or the rubric was ambiguous. Read both rationales before deciding.

Pick the base on which candidate a future maintainer can extend most easily without breaking invariants. Prefer the cleaner boundary or smaller API when two feel tied, per the [Laziness Protocol](../principle-laziness-protocol/SKILL.md).

Record the pick and the reason in a short synthesis note alongside the base artifact, including the cross-judge's verdict.

## Phase E: Graft

Walk each losing candidate once more and identify what is worth porting into the base. The signal is usually one or two things per candidate, not most of it.

Fold each graft in by hand, per [redesign-from-first-principles](../principle-redesign-from-first-principles/SKILL.md). Don't paste mechanically. The result has to remain coherent under one mental model.

Record what was grafted, from which candidate, and what was rejected and why.

When N candidates converge on the same shape, that is a strong agreement signal. Note the convergence in the record and deliver the consensus shape within authorized scope. No graft is needed. When N candidates wildly diverge, Phase A was under-specified. Reframe and re-run rather than averaging the divergence.

## Phase F: Verify

The synthesized artifact has to hold up under the same scrutiny as any other output, per [prove-it-works](../principle-prove-it-works/SKILL.md).

If verification surfaces a problem the arena did not catch, either Phase A was wrong (re-frame and re-run) or one candidate caught it and you missed the graft (go back to Phase E). Don't paper over.

Apply [unslop](../unslop/SKILL.md) to the synthesis prose. External publication, commits, messages and setup require their own authorization.

## Outputs

One synthesized artifact. One short synthesis note alongside, naming the base, the grafts and their source candidates, the rejections, the dropouts if any, and the verification result.

---
name: automate-me
description: "Use for \"automate me\", \"create/update/refresh my -mode skill\", \"turn/capture my preferences or working style into a skill\", or wanting agents to follow how the user works. Drafts or revises a personal -mode skill via create-skill + unslop, optionally pulling fresh evidence from recent transcripts."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Automate me

A guided flow for turning the user's working conventions into a skill agents will follow. The output is one `-mode` skill tailored to them such as `jay-mode` or `priya-mode`.

This flow sequences history mining, an exposed `create-skill` authoring companion, and [unslop](../unslop/SKILL.md). If the companion is absent, disclose it and use the [Authoring or modifying a skill playbook](../poteto-mode/playbooks/authoring-a-skill.md) as an explicit reduced fallback. Read that guidance in full before authoring. Do not claim the missing companion ran.

## Portable prerequisites

Preserve the complete pstack baseline before personal customization. Do not draft or edit a personal mode until every baseline inventory disposition is reviewed and each host has observed evidence for supported behavior or an explicit block. User authorization is a separate requirement and does not satisfy this prerequisite. Before then, explain the workflow and identify the unmet gate without making personal configuration changes.

Discover actual read, history, user-question, worker, execution and write operations through [session capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md). Follow [workflow ownership](../../references/workflow-ownership.md) and the [assignment contract](../../references/orchestration-contract.md). Source invocation aliases and metadata guide invocation; they do not register host APIs. No scheduling or remote creation is part of this flow.

## Flow

### 0. Check for an existing skill

Look recursively in the authorized project and personal skill locations for `*-mode/SKILL.md` matching the user's handle. Preserve an existing source-host project or personal location instead of migrating it implicitly. Discover host skill paths before choosing a new destination. Mode skills can live in a personal category directory under the project skill root, not only at the top level. If one exists, confirm intent with the exposed user-question operation, or a concise chat question if unavailable, unless they already said "update my skill" or similar:

- Update the existing skill. This is the default for repeat runs.
- Start fresh. Ask why before doing this rare reset.

Update mode changes the rest of the flow:
- Step 1 mines only history since the skill was last edited using `git log -1 --format=%cI <path>` when available. If the edit boundary cannot be established, declare the gap and ask for the boundary before mining.
- Step 2 asks what's changed or missing, not what to capture from zero.
- Step 4 edits the existing file in place. Preserve sections the user hasn't contradicted. Revise ones with new evidence. Add new sections only for genuinely new rules.

### 1. Mine their history

Locate the active workspace's transcripts before fanning out. Use only an explicitly supplied workspace transcript path or an observed history binding scoped to that workspace. The source uses the system prompt's `agent-transcripts/` directory. If no scoped history exists, disclose the gap and use user-supplied evidence as reduced capability. Do not glob across the source host's global projects directory. That crosses workspace boundaries and reads private chats from unrelated projects.

Survey recent agent conversations within that scope for recurring patterns. Use multiple independent workers across authorized slices of recent history, such as the last 2-4 weeks split into 3 slices, only when exposed and authorized. Assign distinct slices under the assignment contract and inspect each result. Otherwise mine sequentially as reduced capability, without claiming independence. Each slice mining subagent reads transcripts from the workspace-scoped path the parent provides, looks for the signals below, and returns a short structured list of patterns it saw with evidence pointers. Default signals worth hunting:

- Response preferences (length, tone, format, "dumb it down" corrections)
- Delegation habits (subagents, models, specialized workflows, parallelism)
- Verification posture (what "done" means, unit tests vs live repro, reviewers)
- Code and prose discipline (style, principles cited, lint/format tools)
- Process conventions (worktrees, commits, PRs, review/merge tooling)
- Meta preferences (fixing skills mid-task, proposing new ones)

Cross-check across slices before elevating a signal. Patterns seen in 2+ slices are high-confidence. Lone signals are weak and usually get dropped. Label evidence strength and cite pointers in the findings and draft review. Distinguish repeated observed behavior, a direct user statement, an inference and an unresolved contradiction. Do not silently elevate a weak signal.

### 2. Ask the user directly

Mining misses intent that hasn't come up yet. Use the exposed structured user-question operation when available. Otherwise ask concise chat questions and declare that reduced binding.

Prefer one or two questions with 4-6 options each and multiple selections for categories when the tool supports them. Adapt to the documented option and selection limits without pretending unsupported flags exist. Start broad ("Which areas matter most?"), then follow up on selected areas with specific options. After the structured rounds, one free-form chat question catches anything the options missed.

Don't dump 20 questions.

### 3. Cluster findings

Group the combined signals into sections. Common ones (use only what applies):

- **Response style**: length, tone, format.
- **Autonomy**: how much to do without asking, MCP tool use.
- **Understand first**: which skills to reach for when scoping or investigating a change.
- **Subagents**: default, parallelism, model-to-task, specialized workflows.
- **Prose / code discipline**: principles, lint tools, style guides.
- **Review and verify**: repro posture, verification skills, live-testing tools.
- **Process**: git worktrees, commits, PRs, review/merge tooling.
- **Skills**: skill-authoring habits, fix-the-skill-first, proposing new skills.

The [poteto-mode](../poteto-mode/SKILL.md) skill shows the shape. Read it for granularity. Don't copy its content. The user's rules are not the same as poteto-mode's.

### 4. Draft the skill

Use the exposed `create-skill` companion, or the declared reduced authoring fallback, to prepare the draft. Placement:

- Path: preserve an existing mode skill's category. For a new mode, use `<project-skill-root>/<handle>/<handle>-mode/SKILL.md` when the repo has an established personal category for that handle. Otherwise use the discovered host project skill location, or its personal location if the user chooses it. Changing personal or global configuration requires explicit authorization.
- Handle: the user's first name or chosen identifier.
- Frontmatter `description`: trigger on their name + `/<handle>-mode` + "work in their style", not on generic keywords like "write code" or "review PR".
- Frontmatter formatting: follow `create-skill`'s YAML rules. Keep `description` as one YAML scalar. Quote it or use `description: >-` with indented continuation lines when punctuation or wrapping requires it.
- Frontmatter `disable-model-invocation: true` by default. Opt out only if the user explicitly wants their mode to apply on every turn.

### 5. Iterate on prose

Apply the **unslop** skill and `create-skill`'s writing guidelines to every line.

Show the draft to the user and take feedback before editing the destination. Preserve uncontradicted sections and show the evidence strength and unresolved gaps beside proposed changes. Draft approval authorizes only the agreed scope, not shipping or remote actions. Expect multiple iterations. Cut ruthlessly. A mode skill is not a manual.

### 6. Land it

The source landing contract is a worktree off main, a commit and a PR, never a direct push to main. Prepare the approved local change in an authorized worktree when available. Commit, push and PR creation each require their own authorization and observed tooling. Without those grants, return the local draft or reviewed diff and state the shipping gate. Do not create remotes, schedule runs, install tools or change personal settings incidentally.

## Guardrails

- **Don't overfit to one conversation.** A preference stated once and contradicted another time is noise. Require multiple instances before codifying it.
- **Don't be clever.** Restating other skills' contents, inventing metaphors, or writing "poetic" prose for an agent reader is cost without benefit. Keep it operational.
- **Reference, don't inline.** Other skills the user relies on should appear as path references, not pasted excerpts. Same for any principle docs they maintain elsewhere.
- **Keep sections minimal.** Only add a section if the user has a specific, non-default rule there. "Communicate clearly" is not a section. "Short paragraphs. Tables when comparing options. Bullets only when items are genuinely parallel." is.
- **Name conventions generic.** Use "the user" or "the human" in imperatives, not the author's first name.
- **Don't force symmetry.** If a user has no process rules worth writing down, skip the Process section entirely.

## Evaluation

A `-mode` skill is subjective output. A `create-skill`-style test/iterate benchmark loop isn't useful here. Vibe-check with the user: does it read like them? Did it miss anything? Then follow the separate landing gates.

Run a description-optimization loop only if the skill's trigger accuracy turns out to be a problem in practice.

## When not to use

- User wants a task-specific skill (not working conventions): `create-skill` alone, no mining required.
- User wants to capture one narrow workflow (e.g. "how I write commit messages"). That's a regular skill, not a mode skill.

---
name: benchmark-checklist
description: "Vet a perf measurement (limiter, tuning, limits, errors, repeatability, relevance, and whether the work happened) before you report or act on it. Use when you run a benchmark or report a speedup or regression you measured."

# Benchmark checklist

Use this when you produce a performance number: a PR's before and after, a regression claim, a hillclimb harness, or a library or config choice. [Explain the Number](../principle-explain-the-number/SKILL.md) says why. Answer each question below with evidence from a run, not from a guess about the code.

For a quick ballpark the user asked for, one run is enough. Still check questions 4 and 7, and say that it is one run. Skip the rest unless that run looks wrong. A choice between options is never a ballpark.

## Capability and permission checks

Use [host-capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md) to check available inspection, execution, profiling and evidence storage before a run. Use commands only when exposed and authorized. The commands below are examples for compatible systems; use an available platform equivalent when a command is missing. Do not install profilers or stop unrelated processes without authorization. If a check is unavailable, name it and retain the report gates below. Reviewing supplied artifacts can produce a reduced assessment, but cannot supply missing run evidence. If neither artifacts nor authorized inspection are available, report the measurement as blocked.

Record the workload, data size, concurrency, timed region, exact revisions and configurations of every side, and sample count with the run evidence. Check machine contention, tuning, caches, warmup, errors and completed work before claiming a measured improvement. Preserve `disable-model-invocation: true` as source metadata without assuming the host enforces it.

## Before you run anything

- Write down the claim you expect to make, in the words you would ship ("export is 30% faster at p50 on the 60k-row dataset"). The questions test that sentence.
- Read the measurement script. Note what it times, what it counts, and what it ignores.
- Check the load average with `uptime` and the core count with `nproc`. If the machine is busy, find out what is running. If you cannot stop it, interleave the sides so both see the same noise, and say so in the report.

## The questions

1. **Why not double?** Name the limiter. Profile in a run you do not report, because profilers and tracers slow the work down. Use CPU per process (`top`, `pidstat`), a profiler for the runtime (`node --cpu-prof`, `py-spy`, `perf`), I/O wait, and syscall counts (`strace -c` on Linux). Then map the hot spot to source. Watch the load generator too. If it saturates first, you measured the load generator. If a change did not move the number, the limiter explains why, so find it before you call the change useless.
2. **Was it tuned?** Run every side the way production runs it: release builds, production flags and env, batching and transaction settings, connection pools, caches as warm or cold as production sees them, and the same versions and data. If one side runs on defaults, you compared configurations, not implementations. A limiter that is a setting, such as a commit per row, a debug build, or a missing index, means that side is untuned. Tune it and measure again before you pick a winner. If you cannot tune it, do not pick a winner from that run. Narrowing the claim to the code as it ships today does not fix this when the user is choosing what to adopt, because they adopt the option, not today's settings.
3. **Did it break limits?** Do the arithmetic. Compare bytes per second with disk and network bandwidth, and operations per second times the cost per operation with the cores you have. Compare the time saved with the time the changed piece took. Removing a piece that takes 10% of the run can make the run at most about 11% faster. A result past a limit means the run measured something other than the work, such as a cache, a no-op, or a bug.
4. **Did it error?** Count failures and non-success responses, and check that the outputs are correct, not just present. Errors behave differently from successes. Rejections are often fast, and timeouts and retries are slow. If the script does not count errors, add the count.
5. **Does it reproduce?** Run each side at least 5 times, and alternate the sides (A, B, A, B, and so on) so that warmup, lazy initialization, caches, and drift do not favor one side. Report the median and the range. Treat a gap smaller than the run-to-run variation as no measurable difference. When the call is close, use a rank-sum test or the harness's own statistics.
6. **Does it matter?** Next to any micro result, measure the end-to-end path a user waits on, with realistic data sizes and concurrency. Report the micro result as a share of the whole. A helper that takes 1% of a request can make the request at most 1% faster, however fast the helper gets.
7. **Did it even happen?** Confirm the work ran inside the timed region. The request reached the server, the rows were written, the bytes were read, and the code used the result. Lazy code (generators nobody iterates, promises nobody awaits, results the JIT can discard) and timeouts all produce numbers for work that never happened.

## Report

- Lead with the verdict: faster, slower, no measurable difference, or inconclusive.
- Give the number with its unit, the run count, the range, and the limiter. For example, "p50 41 ms → 33 ms, median of 7 runs per side, range 32 to 35 ms after, bound by JSON parsing on one core."
- Call the verdict inconclusive when you claim a difference but cannot name the limiter, when a side ran untuned, or when you could not check questions 4 and 7. Name the gap.
- Keep a PR body to one primary number, per the **Opening a PR** playbook. Put the runs, the range, and the limiter evidence in a linked artifact or a notes file.

## How this fits the other perf material

- The **Perf issue** playbook finds and fixes slowness, and the performance mantras in its step 2 generate the fixes. This skill vets its baseline before the playbook plans from it, and every number after that.
- The **Hillclimb** playbook loops on one metric. This skill vets its harness before the harness is frozen. The frozen harness then prints error and work counts, so each keep-or-revert checks questions 4 and 7 for free.

# Blast radius

Find what a change breaks somewhere else, before it ships. Use for "blast radius of X", "what could this break", or reviewing a small diff you don't trust yet.

Companion to [how](../how/SKILL.md) and [why](../why/SKILL.md). `how` tells you what the code does. `why` tells you why it's shaped that way. Blast radius tells you what it breaks somewhere else.

Listing the callers is not the job. The agent can grep those in a second. The job is the breakage grep won't show you.

## Don't trust your own writeup

A blast-radius writeup that sounds right is worthless. It reads as convincing whether or not it's true. So don't hand back the writeup. Find the one or two facts the whole thing depends on and prove them by running code.

### How sure are you

For each fact the change's safety depends on, get it as far down this list as is cheap, and say where it stopped.

1. You said so. Worthless on its own.
2. You pointed at the line. A real `file:line`, or the library's own source.
3. You showed the bad case can't happen. You walked the failure step by step and it doesn't reach.
4. You ran it. A script or test that calls the real code and fails loud if you're wrong.
5. You reproduced it in the running app.

Step 4 is usually one small script that imports the same library the app ships and calls the exact function you're worried about.

## Steps

1. Read the change. The diff, the symbols it adds, changes, and deletes, and what it now does differently, including the part the diff doesn't spell out. Use [why](../why/SKILL.md) step 2 to pull the PR and commits through available, authorized source tools. If history is unavailable, state that gap.
2. Find the one fact it's safe because of. Most changes that look risky are safe because of a single fact, like "this call only drops already-dead cache entries and does nothing else". Find that fact. If it holds, most risky cases are cleared at once. Spend your time here, not on a long list of maybes.
3. Look where grep stops. Read the source of the library you call, and check its pinned version and any local patch. Work out when things run: microtasks, unmount and teardown, Solid versus React. Follow what a symbol search misses: the JSON an API returns, a DB column, a wire format, another language reading the same bytes, a feature flag, code three hops downstream.
4. Be honest about each risk. Give it a real chance of happening and a real cost if it does. Keep the risks you confirmed. List the ones you checked and cleared separately. Same rules as `why`. Cite a real `file:line`, a search that finds nothing is still an answer, and never make up a caller or an API.
5. Prove the one fact. Write a script or test that runs the real code, run it, and paste what happened.
6. For a big or wide change, run it as an [arena](../arena/SKILL.md). Ask more than one model the same question and merge the answers. Different models catch different real bugs. Check [session capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md), [model selection](../../references/model-roles.md) and the [assignment contract](../../references/orchestration-contract.md) first. Delegate only when authorized. Record requested and observed models separately. Missing workers or unavailable model diversity require a disclosed reduced-capability review; sequential review does not supply independent workers, and unknown observed models leave diversity unverified.

## Execution and permission limits

Check the current session execution capability and authorization before the proof step. Use the project's available runtime and pinned dependencies. Record the command, exit status and output; source reasoning and an unexecuted script do not prove a runtime consequence. If execution is unavailable or denied, mark the fact unproven, say where the evidence stopped, and provide the cheapest proposed test. If the diff or relevant source is unavailable, report that block without inventing a caller. Missing dependencies remain setup-required; this review does not authorize installation, publishing or external writes.

## What to hand back

- **What it does.** What changed, including the part that isn't obvious.
- **The one fact it's safe because of.** State it, say which step you got it to, and show the proof. If you couldn't prove it, write unproven.
- **Risks.** Each names how it breaks, the `file:line`, how likely and how bad, and how to check. Paste the proof for the ones that matter.
- **Cleared.** What you checked and why it's fine.
- **Before you merge.** The cheapest test or repro that catches the real bug, including the script you wrote.

Write it through [unslop](../unslop/SKILL.md), cite real code, and strip anything private before it goes anywhere public.

**Reply:** the writeup above, with the one safety fact either proven or marked unproven.

# Correct

The operator keeps correcting agents in this repo for the same mistakes. Change the repo so the next agent can't make them.

Assume every contributor is an agent that sees only the files it opened, copies the nearest example, and takes the shortest path that compiles. Design the repo so a change that looks right from one file is right for the whole repo.

## Permissions and capabilities

Use the available repository read, history, write and execution tools under the [session capability contract](../../references/host-capabilities.md). Declare missing history, review comments or CI access. A correction does not authorize edits outside the agreed repository scope.

Before changing durable skills or agent instruction files, present the proposed edit for review and obtain explicit permission. Preserve this gate when updating the rule table. Commits need user authorization, and external actions need their own explicit authorization. If writes or execution are unavailable or unauthorized, report the evidence and proposed enforcement as reduced capability. Do not claim edits, checks or CI results you did not observe. If repository evidence is unavailable, state the block and request the relevant evidence.

## Find the mistake classes

First, read recent commits, reverts, review comments, agent instruction files, and comments that explain workarounds. Group the mistakes into classes. A class counts once it has happened twice.

## Fix each class at the highest level that works

1. **Eliminate it with architecture.** Give each piece of state one owner and each task one supported way. Hide internals so the wrong import fails. Replace hand-synced lists with one source of truth. Delete old ways and dead code an agent would copy.
2. **Enforce it with types so the bad state can't be written.** If bad code still compiles, add a lint or CI check whose error names the file, type, or function to use instead. If the pattern is already common, fail only when a change adds more.
3. **Test the behavior.** Fix or delete any test that would still pass if every function it calls returned nothing.
4. **Write docs or agent rules last, only for judgment calls.** Nothing fails when an agent skips them.

## Fix and prove

Then fix the most frequent classes now within authorized scope, one commit each when commits are authorized. Prove each new check fails on a real past mistake. Run the same command locally and in CI. Exceptions go on the offending line with a reason, an expiry date, and a human's approval.

## Keep the rule table

Last, keep a table in the agent instruction file that pairs each rule with what enforces it. When the operator corrects you, fix the mistake and add the rule. If the rule was already there and nothing enforces it, that's a repeat, so fix it at the highest level in the same change. Drop a rule once its mistake can't happen.

**Reply:** each class with its evidence, the level you picked, and why a higher level didn't work.

# Create a formal verification skill

A test checks the cases that someone thought to write. Formal verification checks every case in a stated scope: every order of steps in a model, every input up to a bound, or every input. This skill finds the part of the repo where that matters most, verifies one property of it, and leaves a project-local skill that lets the next agent check a change against that property. Write that skill for an agent who reads it cold, mid-change, and has never seen your work. The user must be able to trust the result and act on it without learning the verification language.

## Host capabilities and safe execution

Read [host capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md) and [workflow ownership](../../references/workflow-ownership.md). Discover the host's project-local skill location and registration requirements before writing. A file is not proof of discovery. Use only exposed, authorized read, execution, write and persistence operations. Do not install a verifier, download executables, change personal settings, start services, send data externally or schedule maintenance without applicable authorization. Never execute source merely because it was fetched.

Keep the port's [model roles](../../references/model-roles.md) and [assignment contract](../../references/orchestration-contract.md). No new model mappings or worker lifecycle are introduced. Required independent work needs an exposed authorized worker, observed completion and result inspection; a sequential substitute must disclose reduced capability. If a worker is interrupted, inspect its terminal state and quarantine partial artifacts before integration.

Run deliberate broken-code trials only in an owned disposable copy or worktree with isolated data and no shared or external side effects. Record the initial files and check result, revert only the trial's exact edits, rerun the original check, and verify cleanup. Never reset, stash or overwrite user changes. If isolation cannot be established, block the mutation trial and keep validation incomplete. Preserve evidence outside cleanup paths. A timed-out or cancelled run is blocked, never a pass.

ChatGPT and Codex have different session tools. If repository history, execution or durable writes are unavailable, name the missing operation and leave the affected result blocked or an authorized draft. Do not claim a proof, persisted sync point or registered skill from an unrun recipe. Distinguish model-checked bounds, code-level verification, and generated-input/property testing in every handoff; a testing fallback is not formal proof. Accept generated testing skills as maintenance inputs when they state that limitation. Advance a sync point only for code actually inspected and verified by a completed check; if uncommitted covered code remains, record its digest and keep the committed sync point unchanged until a committed revision is rechecked.

## Choose the target from the code

Answer from the codebase, and ask the user only what you cannot observe. If the user named an area or a bug, start there.

A good target is a promise the code makes, where a break harms users and tests rarely reach the case that breaks it. Choose the strongest such target in the repo, not the one that is easiest to verify.

## Let the question choose the tool

Pick the tool that answers the question at the lowest cost: a model checker, a proof assistant, an SMT-backed verifier, or another tool. Whether events can happen in a bad order usually suits a model checker over a small model of the design, and TLA+ is the default for that in any language. Whether the code itself behaves for every input, as with memory safety, overflow, or a data-structure invariant, usually suits a verifier that runs on the code. If no verifier runs on this language, say so, and test the real code with generated inputs, not a hand model of the function. A property that must hold at every size, where a bound is not enough, can need a proof. Prefer a tool that the repo's developers can install and run, and tell the user why you chose it.

## What makes it good

- **True to the code.** Every part of the model or proof points to code that a reviewer can open. What the verification treats as one indivisible step is one indivisible step in the code. Names come from this repo.
- **Able to fail.** A check that you have never seen fail proves nothing. Show each property failing on a broken variant of the code it guards, such as a removed check or a reordered step.
- **Findings stay findings.** When the current code breaks the property, report it with the counterexample in the code's terms. Do not weaken the property or the model until it passes, and do not change product code unless the user asks.
- **Honest about scope.** Say what is verified, under which bounds and assumptions, and what is left out. A pass covers the model or the bound, not the whole system.
- **Readable without the tool.** State the property and the harm in one plain sentence each. Tell a counterexample as a short sequence of steps in the code's words.
- **Cheap to rerun.** One command, a reproducible tool version, and a run short enough that the next agent will use it on every relevant change.
- **Kept in step with the code.** Record which files and functions each check covers, and the commit at which you last confirmed that the verification describes them. When the covered code changes after that commit, the next agent can see that the verification needs another look.

## Generate the verify skill

Write a project-local skill with frontmatter that names the area and says when to use it. Without frontmatter, the skill never registers. From the skill alone, the next agent must be able to tell whether a change touches the verified code, run the check, tell a real bug from a modeling error, and update the verification when a change is intended. Put the coverage record and the sync commit in the skill, and tell the next agent to move the sync commit forward only after it confirms that the verification describes the code at the new commit. Use this repo's real commands, paths, and nouns, and leave no placeholders.

When the check is a TLA+ model, tell the next agent to read its results with [`/statechart`](../statechart/SKILL.md) by name. It reports counterexample paths in reader-facing words and draws the graph within its stated chart budget. Above that budget it may show bug paths only or produce no chart for a passing model. Keep unchecked rules and incomplete runs explicit. Do not copy the helper commands, options or paths into the generated skill or its scripts; read the current skill instead.

## Prove it before you hand off

Follow the generated skill once, as the next agent would, on a scratch change that breaks the property in the real code. It must catch the break. Then drop the scratch change and confirm that the check is back where it started: passing, or failing only on the findings you will report. A verify skill that was never run is a draft. If the skill misses the break or a step does not run, fix the skill or the verification, not the scratch change.

## Hand off

Tell the user what you verified, which tool you used and why, the bounds, what the check found in plain words, how to run it, and what it does not cover. Suggest a second target only if you found a close one. Point the user at `/maintain-formal-verification-skill` for bringing the verification back in line after changes that did not recheck it.

# Create a verification skill

Every serious project needs a scripted way to drive the real app and prove behavior: launch it, exercise a feature the way a user would, and capture evidence. This skill generates that as a project-local skill (`<project-local-skills>/verify-<app>/`) tailored to the repo. You write the generator's output for the next agent, not for a human: it will be read cold, mid-task, by an agent that has never seen the app.

## Host binding and authoring boundaries

Read [host capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md) and [workflow ownership](../../references/workflow-ownership.md). Discover the current host's project-local skill directory and registration requirements from exposed documentation and repository conventions before writing. In this document, `<project-local-skills>` means that observed directory, never a literal output path. If discovery cannot be confirmed, produce an authorized portable draft and mark registration unverified. Preserve the name, description and explicit invocation aliases; invocation metadata does not prove host discovery.

Bind repository reads, authorized local writes, execution and app-driving to exposed tools and observed results. Use an existing harness where available. Missing browser, PTY or execution capabilities remain explicit; documented recipes are not successful operations. Do not install dependencies, change credentials or settings, start listeners, or perform external writes without applicable user authorization. Follow the active owner's scope. When writes are denied, report the blocker without writing.

If app controls can be inspected but proof cannot run, author a draft tied to those actual controls, mark verification `not-run`, and list missing capabilities and unproved paths. Never fill unknown commands or selectors with invented values. A draft is not a verified deliverable.

## 1. Interview the repo, not the user

Answer these from the codebase and only ask the user what you cannot observe:

- **Surface:** what does a user actually touch? A web UI, a CLI/TUI, a desktop app, an API, a mobile app, a library? A repo can have several; pick the primary one and note the rest.
- **Run:** how does the app start locally? Prefer the repo's own documented dev command (package scripts, Makefile, README quickstart). Note ports, env vars, seed data, auth.
- **Drive:** how can an agent interact with it programmatically? Existing harnesses first, Playwright/Cypress specs, expect scripts, PTY helpers, curl-able endpoints, a debug port. Only then pick a generic recipe: browser/CDP for web and Electron, a tmux/PTY harness for CLI/TUI, plain HTTP for services.
- **Observe:** what evidence can be captured? Screenshots, terminal transcripts, response bodies, logs, exit codes, DB state.
- **Isolate:** can two instances run side by side (ports, data dirs, profiles)? If not, say so in the generated skill: refusing to double-drive a shared instance beats corrupting the user's session.

If the checkout doesn't build or start as-is, fix that first (or report it precisely) before generating; a skill written against a broken base teaches wrong steps. When an irrelevant missing asset blocks startup (a static dir the API never serves, a sample config), the generated skill may create it, clearly marked as verification scaffolding, and remove it in cleanup.

## 2. Generate the skill

Write `<project-local-skills>/verify-<app>/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter (`name: verify-<app>` and a `description` that names the app, the surface, and when to reach for it, without frontmatter the skill never registers) and these sections, each grounded in what the interview actually found (no placeholders left):

- **Launch:** the exact command that starts the app for verification, and how to tell it's ready (a log line, a prompt). Launch must reach a usable state from an empty data directory, including migrations and seed data. Ready means usable, not merely that a process answers. A database health check can pass while initialization scripts are still running. Include teardown. For a short-lived CLI or TUI there is no server to keep alive: launch means build the binary (or install deps) once, then start each drive in its own isolated PTY or tmux session.
- **Doctor:** one read-only check that answers "is this instance worth driving?", process up, right version/build, port owned by us, auth valid. An agent runs this first whenever anything looks off.
- **Drive:** the harness recipe with real selectors/commands from this repo, not examples. Prefer stable handles (ARIA labels, data attributes, prompt strings, route paths) over coordinates and tab order.
- **Evidence:** what to capture for a proof and where it goes. State the proof standards: exercise the real user path, not internal setters or test-only endpoints; capture the action and the resulting state, not just the final screen; verify side effects (files written, rows inserted, messages sent) alongside what's visible; mocks only where a production boundary already isolates the external system. When the safe path is a dry-run or test mode, verify what it actually skips by observing (files, network, git refs) rather than trusting its name: some dry-runs still touch the network or open a browser.
- **Cleanup:** how to tear down instances the run created. Never kill by process name; kill what you started. Cleanup removes instances and scratch state, never the evidence: proof artifacts survive the teardown, in a location the skill names.
- **Helpers:** any script the skill ships is executable and its invocation is shown in the skill body. A helper the reader has to reverse-engineer is not a helper.

## 3. Seed the feature map

Create `<project-local-skills>/verify-<app>/features/README.md` plus one file per user-facing feature you can identify (aim for the top 3-5 to start, from routes, commands, menus, or docs). The Notes files are illustrative contracts, not executable instructions for this repo. Preserve their example commands when consulting them, but derive generated commands from the actual app. Follow the shape in [`references/feature-map-example/`](references/feature-map-example/), with a README index and one file per feature. Each file answers, from the user's point of view: what the feature is, how to reach it, how to drive it with the harness, and what observable end state proves it works. The four H2s are `Sub-features`, `How to get to it (user POV)`, `Driving it with <harness>`, and `Gotchas`. If the seed data lacks a precondition that a journey needs, the journey reports a failure and the reason goes in that feature's `Gotchas`. Never weaken the journey to make it pass. The map is the repo's maintained verification source; a proof that drives one convenient entry point is incomplete when the map lists others.

## 4. Prove the generated skill before handing it over

Run its own instructions end to end once: launch, doctor, drive ONE mapped feature (one is enough; the map exists so later runs can cover the rest), capture evidence, clean up. After cleanup, confirm the evidence still exists at the named location, a cleanup that eats the proof fails this step. Fix what fails, and run the generated cleanup after every failed iteration too, so broken attempts don't strand processes and ports. A generated skill that was never executed is a draft, not a deliverable. If verification used a stand-in for the real target, such as a container instead of a fresh VM or a local stack instead of a remote one, list every setup step the stand-in performed that the target will not. Those steps stay unverified until a run on the real target covers them.

## 5. Offer the maintenance loop

Point the user at `/maintain-verification-skill` for keeping the map honest as the app changes. Suggest a cadence only if they ask.

# Figure it out

When the task matches no playbook, design one. The deliverable before any code is the workflow itself: a sequence of phases that scales rigor to the task, runs the scientific method, and leaves a decision trail a human can audit after stepping away.

## Session capabilities and authorization

Read [host capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md), [orchestration contract](../../references/orchestration-contract.md), and [workflow ownership](../../references/workflow-ownership.md). Bind inspection, execution, persistence and any independent workers to exposed tools and observed operations. Use a written checklist if no todo tool exists. Missing evidence or denied operations stay explicit limits. Sequential execution is reduced capability, not independent workers. Do not claim a saved trail without a write and readback. Preserve the invocation metadata without assuming host enforcement.

Proceed within authorized scope. Commits, external writes, publishing and setup require the applicable authorization; autonomy and a long-run checkpoint do not grant it. If a required skill is absent, state the dependency and preserve its named purpose in the designed workflow without claiming to have run it.

## Start

Open a todolist whose first item is to read the Principles section of the **poteto-mode** skill. Then add the phases below as todos.

## Phase A: Frame

Ground first, then commit. Don't start the run until you can state:

- The definition of done as a falsifiable predicate (the **prove-it-works** principle skill).
- Scope, quantified: rough units and effort, plus the blockers grounding surfaced.
- The rigor level, biased high. One-way doors and high blast radius get more. Reversible low-stakes steps get less. Rigor is gates and artifacts, not "try harder".

Present the framing and tradeoffs before committing to a long run. Reversible work proceeds (the **never-block-on-the-human** principle skill), but a multi-hour run earns one checkpoint.

## Phase B: Design the workflow

Decompose into atomic, independently-landable units. Sequence riskiest-unknown-first. Scaffold and verification come before features (the **foundational-thinking** principle skill).

- Build the verification harness before the work, with the baseline captured from the pre-change state, so the check reads as "old value vs new value".
- For one-way-door design decisions, run the **architect** skill (it runs **arena**). Skip it for mechanical work whose shape is already concrete. A second arena over a settled design is over-engineering (the **laziness-protocol** principle skill).
- Decide what fans out. Parallelize only across seams, and give each worker its own worktree or branch (the **separate-before-serializing-shared-state** principle skill). Don't over-fan.
- Write the designed phase list down. That list is what the human reviews.

Then execute the design. Add its steps to the todolist as concrete items, after the Phase C entry and before Phase D. Run each under the Phase C loop discipline, and weave the Phase D log through them, a row as each step lands, rather than saving the whole trail for the end.

## Phase C: Run the loop

Each unit is an experiment. State the hypothesis, make the smallest change, measure against the predicate on the real artifact, keep it if it advanced, revert it if it didn't.
Apply the **sequence-verifiable-units** principle skill, verifying each unit before starting the next instead of batching checks at the end.

- Verify by inspecting the artifact, never a self-report. When something passes too easily, suspect the observation method before the system.
- Pair delegated work with a judge. If a worker games the gate, reset and harden the contract. If the gate itself is wrong, fix the gate in its own change rather than routing around it.
- A verdict is VERIFIED, NOT VERIFIED, or INCONCLUSIVE. Inconclusive is not a pass. Don't hide a negative.

## Phase D: Keep the audit trail

Log the run via the **show-me-your-work** skill. figure-it-out's work is usually ambitious enough to commit the trail so the reviewer can read it in the PR. The trail plus the diff is what lets the human come back and trust the work.

## Phase E: Verify and hand back

Check the whole against the Phase A predicate on the real product, not just the harness. Encode any recurring correction as a gate, a lint rule, a check, or a script (the **encode-lessons-in-structure** principle skill).

**Reply:** the playbook you designed, the rigor level and why, the decision-trail path, what's verified against the predicate, and what's still open.
